questions.prompt: A file declares `interface Config { model: string }` and later `interface Config { maxSteps: number }`. What does TypeScript do, and what if both were `type Config = {...}` instead?

choices.text: Interfaces: a `Duplicate identifier` error. Types: they merge into one shape
Both merge into one shape with `model` and `maxSteps`
Both give a `Duplicate identifier 'Config'` error
Interfaces: they merge into one shape. Types: a `Duplicate identifier` error

questions.explanation: An interface can always be reopened to add properties (declaration merging). A type alias can't be changed after it's created, so a second `type Config` is a duplicate identifier. This is the main difference the Handbook names between the two.

questions.prompt: Compare type aliases and interfaces in TypeScript. When would you use each?

model_answer.summary: They are nearly interchangeable for object shapes. Interfaces can be reopened and extended with `extends`; type aliases can name any type, including unions. The Handbook's rule of thumb is to use `interface` until you need a feature of `type`.
key_points: Almost every feature of an interface is also available with a type alias
An interface can be reopened to add new properties (declaration merging); a type alias can't be changed after it's created
Interfaces extend with `extends`; type aliases combine with intersections (`&`)
A type alias can name any type, such as a union like `"user" | "assistant"`, which an interface can't
Heuristic: use `interface` until you need a feature of `type`

questions.explanation: In practice the choice rarely matters for plain object shapes. You need `type` for unions and other non-object types, and `interface` when a declaration must be extendable, for example to augment a library's types.

questions.prompt: `function printAll(strs: string | string[] | null) { if (typeof strs === "object") { for (const s of strs) console.log(s); } }` What does TypeScript report?

choices.text: Nothing: inside the `if`, the `typeof` check narrows `strs` to `string[]`
An error: `strs` is possibly `null`, since `typeof null` is `"object"`
An error: `typeof` checks can't narrow a union that includes arrays
An error: `for...of` can't iterate `string`, which is still in the union

questions.explanation: In JavaScript `typeof null === "object"`, so the check narrows `strs` to `string[] | null`, not `string[]`. Add an explicit `strs !== null` check, or test with `Array.isArray(strs)`.

questions.prompt: `function greet(name: string | undefined) { if (name) { return `Hi ${name}`; } return "Hi stranger"; }` Which input unexpectedly returns "Hi stranger"?

choices.text: `" "` (a single space)
`"false"`
`""` (an empty string)

questions.explanation: Truthiness narrowing treats `""`, `0`, `NaN`, `0n`, `null` and `undefined` as false. So `if (name)` removes `undefined` but also skips the empty string. Non-empty strings such as `"0"`, `" "` and `"false"` are all truthy. When the empty string is a valid value, check `name !== undefined` instead.

questions.prompt: `type Shape = Circle | Square`, each with a `kind` literal. `getArea` switches on `shape.kind` and its `default` branch has `const _exhaustiveCheck: never = shape;`. You add `Triangle` to `Shape` but don't add a case. What happens?

choices.text: A compile error in `getArea`: `Type 'Triangle' is not assignable to type 'never'`
Nothing until run time, when `getArea` returns `undefined` for triangles
A compile error in the file that declares `Triangle`
TypeScript adds a `triangle` case automatically

questions.explanation: After every handled case, the only type left in `default` is the unhandled `Triangle`, and nothing is assignable to `never`. So the compiler points at the switch you forgot to update. This exhaustiveness check turns a forgotten case into a build error.

questions.prompt: Your agent's model call can return either text or a tool call. Model this as a discriminated union in TypeScript and explain why it's better than one object with optional fields.

model_answer.summary: Give each variant a literal `kind`, so a `switch` on `kind` narrows to the right variant and a `never` check catches any variant you forgot to handle.
key_points: Each member shares a discriminant property with a literal type, for example `{ kind: "text"; text: string } | { kind: "tool_call"; name: string; input: unknown }`
Checking `kind` (with `switch` or `if`) narrows to that member, so its fields can be used without extra checks
One object with optional fields allows impossible combinations (both `text` and `name`, or neither) and forces a check on every field
A `default` branch that assigns the value to `never` makes the compiler flag any variant added later but not handled

questions.explanation: Discriminated unions make illegal states unrepresentable, which matters for model output that can take several shapes. The compiler, not a runtime crash, tells you about a case you forgot.

questions.prompt: Given `function getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K) { return obj[key]; }`, what happens with `getProperty({ a: 1, b: 2 }, "c")`?

choices.text: It compiles and returns `undefined`
It compiles, because `K` is inferred as `string`
A compile error: `"c"` is not assignable to `"a" | "b"`
A run-time `TypeError`

questions.explanation: `K extends keyof T` constrains the key to the object's own keys, here `"a" | "b"`. The constraint makes a misspelt key a compile error instead of a silent `undefined` at run time.

questions.prompt: Compare `function idAny(arg: any): any` with `function id<T>(arg: T): T`. What type does `let n = id(42)` get, and what does `idAny(42)` return?

choices.text: `id(42)` is `number`; `idAny(42)` is `any`, losing the argument's type
Both are `number`, since TypeScript infers the return from the argument
Both are `any`, because generic parameters default to `any`
`id(42)` is `unknown` until narrowed; `idAny(42)` is `number`

questions.explanation: A type parameter captures the argument's type and reuses it for the return type, so the caller keeps `number`. With `any` the return type is `any`, which turns off checking for everything that uses it. That's the Handbook's case for generics.

choices.text: `function f(x: unknown) { const s = x.toUpperCase(); return s; }`
`function f(x: unknown) { const s: string = x; return s.toUpperCase().trim(); }`
`function f(x: unknown) { const n: number = x + 1; return n; }`
`function f(x: unknown) { if (typeof x === "string") return x.toUpperCase(); }`

questions.explanation: Anything can be assigned to `unknown`, but you can't access properties on it, call it, do arithmetic with it, or assign it to a narrower type until you narrow it with `typeof`, `instanceof` or a type predicate. Only option d narrows first. With `any`, all four would compile, and the bad ones would fail at run time.

questions.prompt: `JSON.parse` returns `any`. Why annotate an LLM's parsed output as `const data: unknown = JSON.parse(text)`?

choices.text: `unknown` makes `JSON.parse` check the value against the declared type at run time
`unknown` makes the compiler refuse to use `data` until you narrow or validate it
`unknown` is erased more cheaply than `any`, so the code runs faster
`unknown` makes `JSON.parse` return `undefined` instead of throwing on invalid JSON

questions.explanation: `any` switches off type checking, so `data.answer.trim()` compiles even if the model sent something else, and crashes at run time. `unknown` forces a check first. It adds no run-time behaviour: type annotations are erased when compiled, so you still need a run-time validator such as Zod, and `JSON.parse` still throws on invalid JSON.

questions.prompt: With `"strict": true`, what does TypeScript say about `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`?

choices.text: An error: `Parameter 'a' implicitly has an 'any' type` (and the same for `b`)
Nothing: it infers `number` from the `+`
Nothing: it infers `string | number`
A warning only, because implicit `any` is allowed under `strict`

questions.explanation: When TypeScript can't infer a type it falls back to `any`. `noImplicitAny`, part of `strict`, makes that fallback an error, so you can't lose type checking by accident. Annotate the parameters, for example `(a: number, b: number)`.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between `unknown` and `any`, and say which you would use for data that comes back from an LLM.

model_answer.summary: Both accept any value, but `any` switches off type checking while `unknown` makes you narrow or validate before use. Use `unknown` for model output, then validate it at run time.
key_points: `any` switches off checking: you can access properties, call it and assign it anywhere, and the `any` spreads to what you derive from it
Anything can be assigned to `unknown`, but `unknown` can only be assigned to `unknown` or `any` without narrowing
You can't access properties of, call, or do arithmetic with `unknown` until you narrow it with `typeof`, `instanceof` or a type predicate
Types are erased at run time, so model output also needs run-time validation (for example Zod) before it's trusted

questions.explanation: `unknown` is the type-safe counterpart of `any`: it puts the check where the untrusted data enters your program, instead of letting a wrong assumption travel until it crashes.
